issues.failure_explanation: Lemma 2 asserts that any bounded sequence in $\mathcal{B}_1$ has a subsequence that converges in $H^1(\Omega)$. The proof justifies this solely by noting that $\mathcal{B}_1$ embeds continuously into $H^1(\Omega)$ and $H^1(\Omega)$ embeds compactly into $L^2(\Omega)$. That combination only implies relative compactness of $\mathcal{B}_1$ bounded sequences in $L^2(\Omega)$, not in $H^1(\Omega)$.

failure_location.quote: It follows from the fact that $\mathcal{B}_1$ is continuously embedded into $H^1(\Omega)$, and $H^1(\Omega)$ is compactly embedded into $L^2(\Omega)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Supply the missing compactness argument: since the dictionary of normalized ridge functions is compact in $H^1(\Omega)$, its closed convex hull (the unit ball of $\mathcal{B}_1$) is compact in $H^1(\Omega)$ by Mazur's compactness theorem.
issues.overall_effect: The justification for extracting $H^1(\Omega)$-convergent subsequences from bounded sequences in $\mathcal{B}_1$ fails as written, affecting the convergence arguments in Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 (case ii).
issues.title: Invalid inference in proof of compact embedding of Barron space into Sobolev space
issues.why_classification: The claim of the lemma is mathematically correct; replacing the flawed one-line deduction with Mazur's theorem on the compact dictionary completely restores the lemma without affecting any downstream statements or rates.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: According to Lemma~\ref{convergesubsq}, there exists a convergent subsequence $f_{n(\delta_{k}),k(\delta_{k})}^{\delta_{k}}$ such that $f_{n(\delta_{k}),k(\delta_{k})}^{\delta_{k}}\to f^*$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ as $k\to \infty$. Thus, similar to the proof of Theorem~\ref{main}, approximate solutions $f_{n(\delta),k(\delta)}^{\delta}$ converge to $f^{\dagger}$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ as $\delta \to 0$.

issues.failure_explanation: For regularizer $\mathcal{R}_1$, the proof only establishes that $f_{n(\delta),k(\delta)}^\delta$ is bounded in $H^1(\Omega)$, yielding a subsequence converging to $f^*$ in $L^2(\Omega)$. However, the operator $A$ is only assumed locally Hölder continuous at $f^\dagger$ with respect to the $H^1(\Omega)$-norm (Definition 2). Because $A$ is not assumed continuous with respect to the $L^2(\Omega)$-norm, $L^2(\Omega)$-convergence does not imply $A(f^*) = g$. Additionally, the proof explicitly relies on $r(n) \to +\infty$ to ensure $r(n) \ge c_\rho(f^\dagger)$, but Theorem 2 omits any divergence condition on $r(n)$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the explicit hypotheses that $A: L^2(\Omega) \to \mathcal{Y}$ is continuous and that $\lim_{n\to\infty} r(n) = \infty$ (or $r(n) > c_\rho(f^\dagger)$ for large $n$).
issues.overall_effect: The convergence of $f_{n(\delta),k(\delta)}^\delta \to f^\dagger$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ for $\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}_1$ and the finite termination guarantee are unproven as stated.
issues.title: Missing continuity hypothesis on forward operator and missing growth condition on network radius
issues.why_classification: Adding $L^2$-continuity of $A$ and divergence of $r(n)$ restricts the operator class (excluding problems where $A$ is continuous only on $H^1$), but preserves the proof architecture and convergence conclusions for $L^2$-continuous forward operators.

issues.failure_explanation: In part (c), the proof claims that for fixed $n$, a subsequence in $k$ converges to $f^\dagger$ as $\ell \to \infty$. But each $f_{n,k}$ belongs to $X_{n,\infty}$, which consists of two-layer networks of at most $n$ neurons, so any limit for fixed $n$ must remain in $X_{n,\infty}$. Generically, the exact solution $f^\dagger$ cannot be represented by an $n$-neuron network, so $f_{n,k_\ell}$ cannot converge to $f^\dagger$ as $\ell \to \infty$ for fixed $n$. Furthermore, stability from part (b) required a fixed $\alpha > 0$, whereas in (c) $\alpha_{k,n} \to 0$. The proof provides no joint or diagonal coupling between $n$ and $k$ to establish the stated doubly indexed limit.

issues.failure_explanation: Equation (10) states the upper bound with the term $\tau^{-1} \Phi^{-*}(\tau\alpha)$. However, the proof derives $\alpha \mathcal{E}^\dagger(f_{n,\alpha}^\delta) \le \tau(\delta + C n^{-s/2}) + \alpha \Phi(\tau\delta) + \tau^{-1}\Phi^{-*}(\tau\alpha)$, which after dividing by $\alpha$ must yield $(\tau\alpha)^{-1}\Phi^{-*}(\tau\alpha)$ (as correctly recorded in the proof when defining $H_\delta$). Omitting $\alpha^{-1}$ breaks dimensional homogeneity and prevents balancing to $\mathcal{O}(\Phi(\tau\delta))$ in part (ii). Moreover, the statement defines $\Phi^{-*}$ as the inverse of $\Phi^*(\alpha) := \sup_{t \ge 0} \{\alpha t - \Phi(t)\}$, but for any concave index function with sublinear growth, this supremum is identically $+\infty$. The proof reveals that $\Phi^{-*}$ was meant to denote $(\Phi^{-1})^*$, the Fenchel conjugate of the convex inverse function $\Phi^{-1}$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace $\tau^{-1}\Phi^{-*}(\tau\alpha)$ with $(\tau\alpha)^{-1}(\Phi^{-1})^*(\tau\alpha)$ in (10), update the definition of $\Phi^{-*}$ to denote the Fenchel conjugate of $\Phi^{-1}$, and change the undefined $f$ in the constant $C$ to $f^\dagger$.
issues.overall_effect: The displayed error bound (10) in Theorem 4 is mathematically incorrect as printed and incompatible with the stated definition of $\Phi^{-*}$ and the rate balancing in part (ii).
issues.title: Missing regularization parameter factor and inverted definition of conjugate function in error bound
